title: Ghost Context: Cross-Context Hallucination in Long-Context Language Models
abstract: Language models are routinely given long, multispan inputs assembled from documents, chat history, tool outputs, and memory entries. When the model generates a response, it may draw on spans that are irrelevant to the query and produce a confident, coherent answer grounded in the wrong part of the context. This paper argues that such failures constitute a distinct phenomenon, which we call Ghost Context, and that the existing taxonomy of hallucination does not adequately capture them. A hallucinating model invents information that is absent from context. A model exhibiting Ghost Context uses information that is present but should not influence the current output. The error is not fabrication; it is misattribution. Critically, Ghost Context can occur even when every span in the context is individually authorized for the user and permissible for the application, making it difficult to detect for access control mechanisms and standard faithfulness checks that treat the context as an undifferentiated pool of evidence. We formalize Ghost Context, propose a taxonomy of four interference patterns, describe a mask-and-rerun detection methodology, and outline the security implications for retrieval-augmented generation and agent memory systems. We argue that reliable deployment of long-context models requires distinguishing Ghost Context from conventional hallucination and developing targeted mitigation strategies for cross-context interference.
